diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Analysis

The cost metric counts executed SSA instructions, so the main overhead to attack is per-block work, not per-word work. Each unrolled block pays for a length check, a branch, and a reslice (`xs = xs[16:]`), which compiles to several pointer/len/cap operations. Inside a block, `xs[k]` with constant `k` gets its bounds check removed by the prove pass once `len(xs) >= 16` is known, so the per-word cost is already close to minimal (load, popcount, add).

That makes the amortized loop overhead the remaining lever. Adding a 32-word block before the 16-word loop means that large inputs pay the length check and reslice once per 32 words instead of once per 16. Inputs shorter than 32 words take the same path as before, with one extra compare. I can't measure the effect on the 50 test vectors, so this is a hypothesis to validate by running it, not a guaranteed gain. Correctness is unaffected: the new block only consumes words in order and the tail logic is unchanged.
